To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) we give a simple framework that adapts approximation algorithms for deterministic problems to their respective stochastic versions, (b) we give a general framework for deriving constant-factor approximations for stochastic Steiner tree, stochastic vertex cover and stochastic facility location for arbitrary distributions, (c) we derive improved results for special (product) distribution, and (d) we use the notion of "strict cost-shares" introduced in [5] to derive our results.
(1) the stochastic version of several combinatorial optimization problem is approximable, and (2) this is true even for arbitrary distributions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of approximation algorithms for a class of combinatorial optimization problem under stochastic uncertainty.
stochastic versions of combinatorial optimization and approximation algorithms for these problems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we provide the first approximation algorithms for stochastic combinatorial optimization.
the stochastic version of the problem is at least as hard to approximate as the deterministic version.
we show how to adapt the deterministic algorithm for the Steiner Tree Problem to its stochastic version.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the stochastic version of the above problems can be solved to within an additive factor of σ-1 times the cost of the optimal solution to their deterministic version.

for a large class of stochastic combinatorial problems, we obtain approximation guarantees that are within a factor of 2 of the guarantees for the deterministic problems, and for some special cases, we obtain guarantees matching the guarantees for the corresponding deterministic problem.
we give the first approximation algorithms for stochastic versions of several well-known combinatorial optimization problem.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the stochastic setting is often not much harder than its deterministic counterpart.
the approximation factor is not affected by the randomness in the input.

the stochastic setting can be viewed as an extension of the deterministic one, and that approximation algorithms for deterministic problems can be used to obtain approximations in the stochastic setting.
